stemMd: Which choice most logically completes the text?

options.label: A
options.textMd: the violet plants' advantage in seed production in the meadow does not depend entirely on visits from bumblebees.

options.label: B
options.textMd: bumblebees are drawn to violet flowers mainly because the violet pigment absorbs ultraviolet light.

options.label: C
options.textMd: hand pollination with a fixed amount of pollen produces less seed in this herb than pollination by bumblebees does.

options.label: D
options.textMd: ultraviolet shielding by the pigment is not what gives violet plants their seed advantage in the meadow.

explanationMd:
Start by listing the two explanations the passage puts on the table for why violet plants set more seed in the meadow: bees visit them more, or the pigment shields their developing seeds from ultraviolet light.

Then ask what the experiment holds fixed and what it leaves in place. Netting keeps every insect out and every flower gets the same hand pollination, so the bee explanation is switched off: both colors are pollinated identically. Full sun with the netting letting light through leaves the ultraviolet explanation switched on: if the pigment really shielded the seeds, violet plants should still come out ahead.

Now read the result the sentence supposes: the two colors set *about the same* amount of seed. With only the shielding effect still able to operate, no difference means the shielding effect is not producing the advantage. That is exactly what the option about the pigment's shielding not being what gives violet plants their advantage says.

The strongest trap is the option saying the advantage does not depend entirely on bumblebees. That is Wieland's own hypothesis, and it is what the *opposite* result (violet plants still ahead under the netting) would have suggested. Before choosing, check which result the sentence actually supposes.

distractorRationale.a: This is the conclusion the other possible result would support. If violet plants had still set more seed with bees excluded, something besides bees would be at work; but the sentence supposes equal seed set, which points the other way, toward pollination rather than the pigment.
distractorRationale.b: The experiment excluded bees entirely, so it can say nothing about why bees prefer violet flowers. The passage links the pigment's ultraviolet absorption to protecting seeds, not to attracting bees.
distractorRationale.c: The experiment never compares hand pollination with bee pollination; every flower in it was hand-pollinated. Nothing in the supposed result bears on which method yields more seed.

accessibilityText: Using the passage about Tomasz Wieland's experiment on white- and violet-flowered plants, choose the ending that most logically completes the final sentence, which supposes that violet and white plants set about the same amount of seed when bees are excluded and every flower is hand-pollinated in full sun.

provenance.notes: Original item. The key follows from a null result in a design that switches off one of two explanations; the strongest distractor is the conclusion the opposite result would support.

review.author: wave7-sat-rw-ideas-craft-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The experiment removes bees, equalizes pollen and keeps full sun, so only the UV-shielding factor is left. If seed set is then equal, shielding does not produce the advantage, which is D. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave7-sat-rw-run1) reached the same answer: The experiment removes bees and equalizes pollen while keeping full sun, so only the UV shielding effect remains. Equal seed would mean the pigment's UV shielding does not produce the advantage. A is what a violet advantage under netting would suggest, the opposite result. B and C are not tested by this design.]

review.notes: Author's own solve and uniqueness check: the experiment equalises pollination and leaves ultraviolet exposure in place, so equal seed set means the shielding effect does not produce the advantage; only the option about the pigment's shielding not being what gives violet plants their advantage says this. The option that the advantage does not depend entirely on bumblebees is what a violet-ahead result would suggest; the option about why bees prefer violet is untestable with bees excluded; the option comparing hand and bee pollination has no comparison behind it. Re-solved from the stem alone with the same result. Stretch: harder than a typical hard inference because the learner must work out which of two mechanisms the design disables, then reason from a null result, and the leading distractor is the researcher's own stated hypothesis, which is the correct answer to the mirror-image question. Not published: awaiting a blind independent solve by a second party.
